analysis.one_liner: Bars states from interfering with women traveling out of state for legal abortion services.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 223–205 on July 15, 2022, with 220 of 220 voting Democrats in favor, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court returned abortion regulation to the states, this bill said that no one acting under state law — a prosecutor, an official, a bounty-suit plaintiff — could stop a woman from traveling to another state for a legal abortion, stop a doctor from treating her, or retaliate against anyone who helped her. It also protected the interstate shipment of FDA-approved abortion pills. The Justice Department or the patient herself could sue violators for court orders and damages. The House passed it; the Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who live in states that ban abortion but can get the procedure legally elsewhere, the health care providers who treat them, and the people and organizations that help them travel. The bill shields all of them from state enforcement, lawsuits, and retaliation. Makers and shippers of FDA-approved abortion drugs also gain protected access to interstate markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women in abortion-ban states and their providers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person acting under state law from preventing, restricting, impeding, or retaliating against a provider who performs a legal abortion for an out-of-state patient, or against anyone who helps the provider or the patient [S2] [S4].
Protects the right to cross a state line for a legal abortion and to help someone else do so, and bars interference with the interstate movement of FDA-approved abortion drugs [S2] [S4].
Gives the Attorney General and harmed individuals a right to sue violators for court orders, damages for economic loss and emotional suffering, and attorney's fees [S4].

analysis.who_pays: State governments and officials in states that ban abortion lose much of their ability to enforce those bans against out-of-state travel, out-of-state care, and the people who facilitate it, and they face lawsuits if they try.

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches any person 'acting under color of state law,' which sweeping language opponents said would override state abortion laws well beyond the travel context; the text covers providers, helpers, travelers, and the movement of abortion drugs in interstate commerce [S4].

It creates a private right of action with compensatory damages including emotional suffering, which would expose state officials and enforcement actors to personal lawsuits; critics argued this shifts enforcement power from states to federal courts [S4].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill does not help women who cannot afford to travel out of state at all — it protects the right to travel, not access to care at home.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the women most affected — those in states with bans — the bill offered concrete, enforceable protection for a right the Supreme Court had just withdrawn from federal protection: to cross a state line for care without being tracked, sued, or punished. The costs fall on states seeking to extend their bans across borders, and the bill's breadth invited constitutional challenges. Its main limitation is that it does nothing for women who cannot travel.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on July 15, 2022, and the Senate received it three days later, but no senator ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 7, 2022 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S6].

The House considered it under a rule reported on July 13, debated it on July 15, rejected a Republican motion to recommit 209–219 (Roll no. 361), and passed it 223–205 (Roll no. 362), with 220 of 220 voting Democrats in favor and only 3 of 208 voting Republicans [S6] [S7] [S8].
The Senate received the bill on July 18, 2022, and the action history records no further action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials in abortion-ban states are better off because the bill died: their authority to enforce bans against out-of-state travel, care, and facilitation was never overridden. Conversely, women in ban states never got the promised federal protection for crossing state lines.

for.name: Rep. Lizzie Fletcher
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member

against.name: Rep. Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee, seeking to return it without a final vote; the motion failed 209–219 (Roll no. 361)

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.role: Senate Majority and Minority leadership, 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor after the Senate received it on July 18, 2022; no vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: all 220 voting Democrats voted yes, while 205 of 208 voting Republicans voted no (3 Republicans crossed over), and the bill then died without any Senate action [S8].

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful under state color of law to impede or retaliate against providers serving out-of-state patients, with federal court backing and damages. Providers gain legal protection for expanding care to women from ban states [S2] [S4].

State officials, prosecutors, and bounty-suit mechanisms lose the ability to police out-of-state travel, out-of-state care, and helpers, and become targets of federal suits. Their interest runs directly against the travel access the bill protects [S2] [S4].

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical makers and distributors of FDA-approved abortion drugs
industries.note: The bill bars state-law interference with interstate movement of FDA-approved pregnancy-terminating drugs, protecting their national distribution channels [S2] [S4].
